headline_en: Investing in technical education will change the economy
summary_en: An opinion piece by a Satkhira polytechnic instructor arguing that Bangladesh should invest in technical education so that migrant workers go abroad with training and recognised certificates and earn more. It cites the skill mix of Bangladeshis who went abroad in 2025 and the under-used network of technical institutions.

facts.statement: According to 2025 figures cited in a Prothom Alo opinion piece, about 43 percent of Bangladeshis going abroad were low-skilled and 34 percent semi-skilled, i.e. roughly seven in ten.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Md. Mamun Hasan, instructor at Satkhira Government Polytechnic Institute

facts.statement: A Prothom Alo opinion piece of 12 Oct 2026 says Bangladesh's annual remittance has crossed USD 30 billion and that Bangladesh is one of the world's largest remittance-receiving countries.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Md. Mamun Hasan, instructor at Satkhira Government Polytechnic Institute

facts.statement: The writer says a worker who goes abroad without the necessary training and a recognised certificate generally stays in the low-skilled or semi-skilled category, and that sending the same people with better training, technical skills and internationally recognised certificates would raise earnings without raising the number of migrants.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Md. Mamun Hasan, instructor at Satkhira Government Polytechnic Institute

facts.statement: Bangladesh has about 12,932 institutions at various levels offering technical education and training; of the 3,440 vocational institutions approved by the Technical Education Board, 621 did not admit a single student in the last five years (as stated in a 12 Oct 2026 opinion piece).
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Md. Mamun Hasan, instructor at Satkhira Government Polytechnic Institute

facts.statement: The writer cites the dual training systems of Germany and South Korea, where industry is a direct partner in training and students gain workplace experience (often as apprentices) alongside classroom study, as a model for Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Md. Mamun Hasan, instructor at Satkhira Government Polytechnic Institute

facts.statement: The writer says demand for technology-skilled workers is rising in textiles, construction, agro-processing, IT, tourism, hospitality and services, and that many countries face a shortage of skilled technical manpower, which he calls an opportunity for Bangladesh if polytechnics update curricula.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Md. Mamun Hasan, instructor at Satkhira Government Polytechnic Institute

headline_en: No compromise on the security of Makkah and Madinah: Humayun Kabir
summary_en: After a seminar on Bangladesh-Saudi relations in Dhaka on 10 Oct 2026, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humayun Kabir said Bangladesh would give Saudi Arabia any help it asks for to protect the holy sites in the context of Houthi attacks. He said the relationship is being widened beyond labour and remittance, and that talks on sending skilled and professional workers are going positively.

facts.statement: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humayun Kabir said on 10 Oct 2026 that Bangladesh is in positive discussions with Saudi Arabia on exporting skilled and professional manpower.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humayun Kabir

facts.statement: Humayun Kabir said the Bangladesh-Saudi relationship earlier depended mainly on sending workers and on remittance, and is now being made more modern and multi-dimensional with cooperation in energy, technology, investment and other sectors.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humayun Kabir

facts.statement: In the context of attacks by Yemen's armed Houthi group, Humayun Kabir said Bangladesh is ready to give any help Saudi Arabia asks for to protect Makkah and Madinah; asked whether there was a plan to send Bangladeshi troops, he repeated that Bangladesh is ready to give any necessary help if asked. He said Bangladesh has already expressed interest in joining the 'Makkah agreement'.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humayun Kabir

facts.statement: Humayun Kabir said the Prime Minister will visit Saudi Arabia but the date is not final. The seminar, 'From workforce to strategic partnership: reimagining Bangladesh-Saudi Arabia relations', was organised by BIISS and North South University at the Foreign Service Academy, Dhaka.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humayun Kabir

headline_en: Haal Fashion lifestyle guideline: what an immigration officer can and cannot ask you, and what to do if harassed
summary_en: A legal explainer, prompted by three unmarried women being stopped at Dhaka airport on 8 August while travelling to Nepal, on what Bangladeshi immigration officers may check and ask at departure and what they may not. It lists the documents a departing traveller needs (including BMET clearance for those going for work), cites constitutional rights to leave and return, and sets out how and where to complain about harassment, including a 24-hour airport immigration hotline.

facts.statement: Three unmarried Bangladeshi women with valid passports, visa or entry permission and air tickets for Nepal were stopped from travelling at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on 8 August; they alleged that immigration police phoned their guardians to ask about their travel and profession and made 'indecent' remarks about their clothes, financial means and personal matters. One said an immigration police member told her unmarried girls cannot go abroad alone.
facts.source_in_article: the three women, in statements to police

facts.statement: Immigration in Bangladesh is not governed by a single law but by a combination including the Overseas Employment and Migrants Act 2013 (and its 2023 amendment), the Foreigners Act 1946, the Citizenship Act 1951, the Bangladesh Passport Order 1973 and travel rules. The Ministry of Home Affairs has overall responsibility; the Department of Immigration and Passports (DIP) issues passports, processes visas and runs immigration services.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: A Bangladeshi immigration officer may examine passport, visa, ticket and other required papers of departing and arriving passengers; ask about the purpose of travel, length of stay and other information and verify it; and detect, detain and take legal action against users of forged papers. Officers may also verify risks of human trafficking, forged documents, a criminal leaving or a legal ban, and question a passenger on reasonable suspicion based on facts, law and professional standards.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: According to the writer, whether a traveller is unmarried, why she is travelling alone, where her husband is, who her guardian is or whether the guardian knows are not relevant questions for an immigration officer; security checks are not the same as intrusion into private life or moral policing.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: To travel abroad legally from Bangladesh a passport and visa are needed; the passport must have at least 6 months' validity and the destination visa must be correct and valid. The traveller needs the airline boarding pass from check-in and a completed departure immigration form.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: Additional papers at departure from Bangladesh: an employee needs an official ID card and an NOC (no-objection certificate); a businessperson a trade licence; a student a student ID or a leave/permission letter from the college or university; a person going for work needs BMET clearance (Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training); other specific travel categories need their relevant papers.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: An immigration officer in Bangladesh may ask why a citizen is going abroad, the destination, where and with whom they will stay or whether there is a hotel booking, and the travel plan; and may ask to see a return flight ticket and proof of enough foreign currency, cash, an international credit or debit card, or a bank solvency certificate/statement.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: The writer states that if a citizen has a valid passport, valid visa, correct air ticket, hotel reservation, a lawful purpose and other travel papers in order, stopping their travel abroad is illegal. The Appellate Division of the Bangladesh Supreme Court has held that no citizen's lawful foreign travel can be blocked without a court ban on travel; a criminal case alone is not enough, and even a convicted person on bail pending appeal may travel if there is no court ban. The same rule applies regardless of marital status, religion, caste or sex.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: Constitutional provisions cited: Article 27 (equality before law), Article 28 (no discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth; equal rights of women and men in state and public life), Articles 31 and 32 (protection of law; life and personal liberty), and Article 36 (right to move freely, to leave Bangladesh and to re-enter, subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by law in the public interest). Restricting a person's freedom by executive order alone without legal backing would be unconstitutional.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: If harassed at immigration or an airport in Bangladesh: complain immediately, in writing and orally, to the senior authority or the Superintendent of Police; stay calm without arguing and note the officer's name, rank or badge number, the time and the counter number; keep specific proof or documents if possible. The matter can be reported at once to the airport's complaint-settlement officer, the shift in-charge, the duty officer or the officer-in-charge (OC) of that immigration post.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: The airport immigration 24-hour hotline number in Bangladesh, as printed, is 01320007588.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: Other complaint routes for immigration harassment in Bangladesh: Special Branch (police) Immigration, the Bangladesh Police portal or the relevant control number; a written complaint with specific details to the airport or Special Branch Immigration; the police immigration online complaint page; an application to the office of the executive magistrate present at the airport; and the national Grievance Redress System (GRS) online platform for dissatisfaction with a government service.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: If none of the complaint routes gives a remedy, a writ can be filed in the High Court Division of the Bangladesh Supreme Court; a complaint must first have been lodged with the proper authority before filing the writ.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

headline_en: Higher study in New Zealand: 24 qualifications make you eligible for the post-study work visa
summary_en: New Zealand is widening eligibility for its post-study work visa for certain graduates from 16 November 2026 and introducing a six-month Short-Term Graduate Work Visa for those who do not qualify. Immigration New Zealand has published a 2026 list of 24 approved qualifications, from Level 4 certificates to Level 7 graduate diplomas, in engineering, construction, education and agriculture, with work limited to jobs directly related to the study.

facts.statement: From 16 November 2026 New Zealand is expanding post-study work visa eligibility for specified graduates.
facts.source_in_article: the article (Prothom Alo report on Immigration New Zealand's announcement)

facts.statement: Alongside the expansion, New Zealand will introduce a new six-month 'Short-Term Graduate Work Visa' for those who are not eligible for the post-study work visa.
facts.source_in_article: the article (Prothom Alo report on Immigration New Zealand's announcement)

facts.statement: Immigration New Zealand has published a list of 24 approved educational qualifications for post-study work visa eligibility for 2026, ranging from Level 4 certificates to Level 7 graduate diplomas, covering graduates in engineering, construction, education and agriculture.
facts.source_in_article: the article (Prothom Alo report on Immigration New Zealand's announcement)

facts.statement: Under the New Zealand Qualifications Framework (NZQF), students who complete a non-degree course at Level 7 or below may only work in jobs directly related to their study; the job after qualifying must be in the relevant field.
facts.source_in_article: the article (Prothom Alo report on Immigration New Zealand's announcement)

facts.statement: Listed New Zealand qualifications and linked jobs include: Level 7 Graduate Diploma in Highway or Civil Engineering (construction project manager); Level 7 Graduate Diploma in Construction Management or Project Management (project manager or builder); Level 7 Graduate Diploma in Quantity Surveying (quantity surveyor); Level 6 Diploma in Engineering - civil, electrical, electronics or mechanical (relevant technician posts).
facts.source_in_article: the article (Prothom Alo report on Immigration New Zealand's announcement)

facts.statement: Further listed New Zealand qualifications: Level 5 or higher Diploma in Farm Management, Agriculture or Dairy Technology (dairy cattle farmer); Level 4 Certificate in Automotive Electrical Engineering or Heavy Automotive Engineering (automotive electrician or diesel mechanic); Level 4 Certificate in Agriculture - dairy or livestock farming (dairy cattle farmer).
facts.source_in_article: the article (Prothom Alo report on Immigration New Zealand's announcement)

facts.statement: A graduate diploma in education on the New Zealand list allows work as a primary, secondary or early-childhood teacher subject to approval by the Teaching Council of New Zealand; the diploma alone is not enough, and applicants must complete the Teaching Council's registration and certification process.
facts.source_in_article: the article (Prothom Alo report on Immigration New Zealand's announcement)

facts.statement: IDP Education Bangladesh's Anwar Hossain said that for these (short, non-degree) qualifications the New Zealand post-study work visa lasts at most one year, whereas students who take a higher university degree can get a post-study work visa of up to three years, subject to meeting the applicable conditions.
facts.source_in_article: Anwar Hossain, Head of Sales and Operation, IDP Education Bangladesh Private Limited

facts.statement: IDP Education Bangladesh's Anwar Hossain said the New Zealand change creates a new opportunity for Bangladeshi graduates who want to finish study quickly and enter the job market, but students should choose a route according to their own qualifications, financial means and long-term career plan.
facts.source_in_article: Anwar Hossain, Head of Sales and Operation, IDP Education Bangladesh Private Limited

headline_en: Government-channel jobs in Brunei, 279 to be hired

The notice gives wages by company and post, the BDT 200 application fee, BOESL's service charge for skilled and semi-skilled/unskilled workers, and contract terms.

facts.source_in_article: BOESL recruitment notice as reported by Prothom Alo

headline_en: A rare diplomatic opportunity before Bangladesh
summary_en: An opinion column on the 81st UN General Assembly session, presided over by Bangladesh's foreign minister Khalilur Rahman, arguing what Bangladesh should press for: Rohingya repatriation, a smooth LDC graduation, trade ties and migration. On migration, the writer says Bangladesh should move the discussion beyond remittance to migrants' rights, recruitment costs, wage theft, skills recognition and reintegration.

facts.statement: Writing about the 81st UN General Assembly, Professor A K M Ahsan Ullah argues Bangladesh's position in international migration talks often stops at remittance, and should move to migrants' rights, excessive recruitment costs, wage theft, recognition of skills, portability of social protection, safe migration routes and reintegration of returning migrants.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Dr A K M Ahsan Ullah, professor at Universiti Brunei Darussalam

facts.statement: The writer says labour demand in many European and East Asian countries is changing because of artificial intelligence, automation and demographic change, and Bangladesh needs market-driven 'skills diplomacy' - partnerships on skills, not just sending people.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Dr A K M Ahsan Ullah, professor at Universiti Brunei Darussalam

facts.statement: Background stated in the column: Khalilur Rahman, Bangladesh's foreign minister, was elected President of the 81st UN General Assembly on 2 June with 99 votes against 91 for Cyprus's candidate; Prime Minister Tarique Rahman took office on 17 February 2026; Bangladesh is scheduled to leave the least-developed-country list on 24 November 2026 but has asked for a longer preparation period.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Dr A K M Ahsan Ullah, professor at Universiti Brunei Darussalam

headline_en: Killed in Saudi Arabia fire: joint funeral for seven in Atrai
summary_en: Sixteen Bangladeshi workers died in a fire at a sofa factory in Manfuha, Riyadh on 9 August 2026. Saudi authorities identified nine by fingerprint; their bodies reached Dhaka on 27 August and were buried on 28 August in Naogaon (seven from Atrai), Rajshahi and Natore, while seven remain unidentified and DNA testing is under way. Families describe the debts taken to send the men, and one victim sent through brokers had no iqama for his first three years.

facts.statement: On 9 August (2026) a fire at a sofa-making factory in the Manfuha area of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia killed 16 Bangladeshi workers.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

facts.statement: After the Riyadh sofa factory fire, Saudi authorities identified nine of the 16 Bangladeshi dead by fingerprint testing; seven were still unidentified as of 28 August 2026, and DNA testing was being used to try to identify them.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report; Naogaon Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Saiful Islam

facts.statement: The bodies of the nine identified victims of the Riyadh fire arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight at about 4:30 pm on Thursday 27 August 2026. (The article's opening sentence says eight identified bodies were buried, but it lists nine: seven from Atrai, one from Bagmara and one from Naldanga.)
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

facts.statement: Seven victims from Atrai upazila, Naogaon had a joint funeral at 10 am on Friday 28 August 2026 at Molla Azad Memorial Government College ground: Md. Farid (Udonpoi village), Rubel Pramanik, Kalimuddin Islam, Mohon Ali and his younger brother Sumon Ali (Gandagohali village), Sohel Rana (Dubai village) and Abdul Jalil Sarkar (Parkasunda village).
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

facts.statement: Naogaon Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Saiful Islam said the process of identifying the remaining six Naogaon residents killed in the Riyadh fire and bringing their bodies home was under way, with identification being attempted by DNA test. Among the unidentified is Minhaj of Madhyaboali village, Atrai, whose mother Parul Bibi appealed to the government to bring his body quickly.
facts.source_in_article: Naogaon Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Saiful Islam; Parul Bibi

facts.statement: Naldanga (Natore) acting UNO Shamim Hossain said that, besides Rabiul Islam, two others from Khajura union died in the same Riyadh fire - Shamim Hossain (35), son of Zakir Ali of Dighirpar village, and Sabbir Hossain, son of Golam Rabbani of Sripurpara - and their bodies had not yet been identified, so could not be brought home.
facts.source_in_article: Naldanga acting UNO Shamim Hossain

facts.statement: Rabiul Islam (28) of Naldanga, Natore was sent to Saudi Arabia five years before his death in August 2026 with a loan of BDT 5 lakh, according to his father Ashraful Islam; part of the loan was repaid from his remittances and the rest remains unpaid.
facts.source_in_article: his father Ashraful Islam

facts.statement: Rabiul Islam went to Saudi Arabia through a broker ring and did not get an iqama (residence permit) for the first three years, so he could not work regularly or earn much, his father said.
facts.source_in_article: his father Ashraful Islam

facts.statement: Shyamal Uddin Majhi (46) of Marugram Dangapara village, Jhikra union, Bagmara, Rajshahi, a father of three daughters, went to Saudi Arabia eight years earlier on borrowed money and died in the Riyadh fire; his coffin was opened in the presence of police at about 10:30 am on 28 August 2026 and the family is worried about repaying his debts. A related headline in the article says he had been due to return home that week after 8 years.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo reporter; family

facts.statement: Former Jhikra union chairman and BNP leader Saiduzzaman thanked the government for bringing Shyamal Uddin's body home quickly and demanded government financial assistance for the family; the article does not report any assistance having been paid.
facts.source_in_article: Saiduzzaman

headline_en: Prime Minister's Malaysia visit: a new horizon of partnership on the East Asian model
summary_en: An opinion column on Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's June 2026 visit to Malaysia arguing the two countries should move from the cheap, unskilled 'manpower export' model damaged by middlemen and syndicates to a skills- and knowledge-based partnership. It proposes post-study work rights for Bangladeshi students, sending technicians to Malaysia's semiconductor industry, and notes that the joint statement included a Bangladeshi proposal for a 'Talent Cooperation Framework'.

facts.statement: The writer says the old 'manpower export' model between Bangladesh and Malaysia - Bangladesh supplying cheap unskilled labour - has damaged both countries' image through middlemen and syndicates.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, M Niaz Asadullah, economics professor at Dhaka University and formerly at Universiti Malaya

facts.statement: According to the column, Bangladeshi students are the second-largest source of international-student tuition income for Malaysian universities; a large share of the top 2 percent most-cited foreign researchers in Malaysia are Bangladeshi academics; and Bangladesh ranks second in capital invested under Malaysia's MM2H scheme.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, M Niaz Asadullah, economics professor at Dhaka University and formerly at Universiti Malaya

facts.statement: The writer says his own move from the UK to Malaysia was eased by the Malaysian government's 'Residence Pass-Talent' scheme, and that Bangladesh has no equivalent scheme to attract talent home.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, M Niaz Asadullah, economics professor at Dhaka University and formerly at Universiti Malaya

facts.statement: The writer proposes a 'Graduate Plus' initiative giving merit-based post-study work rights to Bangladeshi students in Malaysia, and a special agreement to place Bangladeshi engineers and polytechnic graduates in Malaysia's chip-packaging and semiconductor industry: a state-funded pilot of 300 people leading to 30,000 technicians over 10 years, which he estimates could earn about USD 10 billion (the article prints 'BDT 18 thousand crore'). These are the writer's proposals, not decisions.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, M Niaz Asadullah, economics professor at Dhaka University and formerly at Universiti Malaya

facts.statement: The column says Malaysia's technology and data-centre sector has a gap of about 60,000 skilled engineers that Bangladeshi IT and engineering graduates could help fill.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, M Niaz Asadullah, economics professor at Dhaka University and formerly at Universiti Malaya

facts.statement: According to the column, the joint statement after the Putrajaya meeting of the two prime ministers shows agreement on linking Malaysia's semiconductor packaging industry with Bangladesh's IT sector, and Bangladesh's Prime Minister proposed a bilateral 'Talent Cooperation Framework' to skill engineering graduates.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, M Niaz Asadullah, economics professor at Dhaka University and formerly at Universiti Malaya

facts.statement: The writer attended an early-June 2026 event of the Dhaka University Alumni Association Malaysia (DUAM) in Kuala Lumpur and says young Bangladeshi entrepreneurs in AI and big data serve high-level public and private clients in Malaysia, but no Bangladeshi state initiative supports them.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, M Niaz Asadullah, economics professor at Dhaka University and formerly at Universiti Malaya

facts.statement: Malaysia was the first foreign visit of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman after the February 2026 election; Malaysian PM Anwar Ibrahim had visited Dhaka in late 2024 and Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus later visited Malaysia, but the writer says those visits stayed at protocol and paper MoUs.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, M Niaz Asadullah, economics professor at Dhaka University and formerly at Universiti Malaya

headline_en: Bangladesh and Malaysia sign one MoU, exchange two documents
summary_en: On 22 June 2026 Prime Minister Tarique Rahman met Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim at Perdana Putra, Putrajaya. A cultural MoU was signed and documents on counter-terrorism cooperation and investment were exchanged. The talks gave weight to reopening Malaysia's labour market to Bangladeshi workers and to regularising Bangladeshis who had become irregular and renewing work permits; the article reports discussion, not an agreed outcome, on these.

facts.statement: At the Bangladesh-Malaysia prime ministers' talks in Putrajaya on 22 June 2026, reopening the Malaysian labour market for recruitment of Bangladeshi workers was among the issues given importance; the article reports it as a topic of discussion and does not report a decision.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

facts.statement: The 22 June 2026 Bangladesh-Malaysia talks also covered regularisation of Bangladeshi nationals who had become irregular ('illegal') for various reasons and renewal of work permits; the article does not report a decision.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

facts.statement: After the 22 June 2026 talks, an MoU on culture was signed in the presence of both prime ministers, and the two foreign ministers exchanged a document on cooperation in counter-terrorism research and capacity building and a bilateral document on investment. No labour MoU is reported as signed.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

facts.statement: Other topics at the talks: greater access for Bangladeshi mangoes, fruit and vegetables to the Malaysian market, Bangladesh's application to become an ASEAN Sectoral Dialogue Partner, Bangladesh's inclusion in the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, the Rohingya issue, and cooperation at the UN and other multilateral forums.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

facts.statement: The Bangladesh delegation at the talks included Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, among others. Tarique Rahman arrived in Kuala Lumpur at 8:45 pm local time on Sunday 21 June 2026; it was his first state visit since taking office on 17 February.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

headline_en: Krishi Bank now top in remittance; Islami Bank drops to second place
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank data for the first 13 days of June 2026 show Bangladesh Krishi Bank overtaking Islami Bank as the top remittance-receiving bank, after Bangladesh Bank dissolved Islami Bank's board and took over the bank amid customer protests and panic. Overall remittance was not affected. Islami Bank waived charges for old customers and its acting MD apologised to remittance customers, though cheque clearing and ATMs were not yet fully working.

facts.statement: In the first 13 days of June 2026, Bangladesh Krishi Bank received the most remittance of any bank, USD 23 crore 40 lakh (২৩ কোটি ৪০ লাখ ডলার), followed by Islami Bank with USD 21 crore 30 lakh.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank report cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Total remittance to Bangladesh in the first 15 days of June 2026 was USD 162 crore, against USD 148 crore in the same period the previous year; the Islami Bank crisis had not yet affected overall remittance.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank report cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: On Sunday night (about 14 June 2026) Bangladesh Bank dissolved the board of Islami Bank and took charge of the bank, after sustained protests by a group of customers, heated debate in parliament and customer panic; many customers closed accounts and many expatriates turned away from the bank. Islami Bank had been the top remittance-collecting bank since its founding.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

facts.statement: After Bangladesh Bank took over, withdrawal pressure on Islami Bank eased; the bank waived charges for old customers and customers who had closed accounts began returning, but its cheque settlement and ATM systems were not yet fully operational as of 16 June 2026.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

facts.statement: Islami Bank's acting managing director Altaf Hussain, in a video message on the bank's social media, apologised for the temporary difficulties faced by remittance customers and urged them to keep sending remittance through Islami Bank without fear.
facts.source_in_article: Altaf Hussain, acting MD, Islami Bank

headline_en: Why Ziaur Rahman's foreign policy was different
summary_en: A column, condensed from a speech marking Ziaur Rahman's 45th death anniversary, on his foreign policy. Its only migration-related content is historical: it credits his ties with Middle Eastern and South-East Asian countries with opening labour markets for Bangladeshis and says BMET was established in 1976.

facts.statement: According to the column, BMET (Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training) was established in 1976 under President Ziaur Rahman, bringing labour migration within an institutional framework.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Maj Gen (retd) A N M Muniruzzaman, president of the Bangladesh Institute of Peace and Security Studies

facts.statement: The column says Ziaur Rahman's improved relations with Middle Eastern countries, especially Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates, opened foreign labour markets to Bangladeshi workers and laid the base of the remittance economy, and that his 1976 visit to Malaysia and ties with ASEAN countries created job opportunities in Malaysia, Singapore and other South-East Asian labour markets.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Maj Gen (retd) A N M Muniruzzaman, president of the Bangladesh Institute of Peace and Security Studies

headline_en: Bangladesh's labour market in Mauritius is about to reopen
summary_en: At a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the 114th International Labour Conference in Geneva on Monday 8 June 2026, Bangladesh's expatriates' welfare minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury and Mauritius's labour minister agreed in principle to sign an MoU quickly so that the long-closed Mauritius labour market reopens to Bangladeshi workers. Mauritius said it would send a draft MoU soon and that its textile industry needs many skilled workers.

facts.statement: After being closed for a long time, the Mauritius labour market for Bangladeshi workers is set to reopen: on 8 June 2026 in Geneva, Bangladesh and Mauritius agreed in principle to sign a memorandum of understanding (MoU) quickly on manpower export. The MoU had not yet been signed.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report of the bilateral meeting

facts.statement: Mauritius's labour minister Muhammad Reza Cassam Uteem (মুহাম্মদ রেজা কাসাম উতিম) said his country is very keen to take skilled workers from Bangladesh, that the Mauritian textile industry in particular needs many skilled workers, and that a draft MoU would be sent soon to reopen the labour market.
facts.source_in_article: Mauritius labour minister

facts.statement: Bangladesh's expatriates' welfare minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury asked Mauritius to sign the MoU quickly and said Bangladesh is ready to send, besides textile workers, skilled doctors, engineers, nurses and other professionals; he invited the Mauritian labour minister to visit Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury

facts.statement: The meeting also discussed the current situation of Bangladeshi workers in Mauritius; the Mauritian minister expressed interest in investing in Bangladesh's textile sector. Bangladesh's delegation included Labour and Employment Secretary Md. Abdur Rahman Tarafder and Ambassador to Switzerland Nahida Sobhan.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

headline_en: Three MPs visit the families on behalf of the Prime Minister
summary_en: Three Sunamganj MPs visited, on the Prime Minister's behalf on Sunday 5 April 2026, the families of 13 Sunamganj men who died on a rubber boat in the Mediterranean while going from Libya to Greece. The boat left on 21 March, lost its way, ran out of fuel and drifted six days; 22 people died of lack of food and water, 18 of them Bangladeshis. The MPs gave condolences and some gifts and urged people not to go abroad irregularly.

facts.statement: A rubber boat that set out from Libya for Greece on 21 March (2026) lost its way in the Mediterranean, stayed at sea six days and ran out of fuel; 22 people on board died from lack of food and water.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

facts.statement: Of the 22 dead on the Libya-Greece boat, 18 were Bangladeshis, 13 of them from Sunamganj: six from Derai upazila, five from Jagannathpur, one from Dowarabazar and one from Chhatak.

facts.statement: Sunamganj-5 MP Kalim Uddin Ahmad said the families' loss is irreparable and that no one should go abroad illegally like this; those who go abroad should go legally, not by risking their lives.

headline_en: Masud Uddin is shifting blame for one-eleven onto others
summary_en: Retired Lt Gen Masud Uddin Chowdhury, known as a key figure of the 2007 'one-eleven' emergency, is being interrogated on remand by Dhaka's Detective Branch in a human trafficking case filed at Paltan police station, and is also being asked about his 2007 role, for which he blames others. Police say a syndicate in manpower export shut out other licensed agencies and took extra money from workers going abroad, and that his company was part of it.

facts.statement: Lt Gen (retd) Masud Uddin Chowdhury was arrested from his Dhaka home on a Monday night (about 23 March 2026) and the next day (Tuesday) a court gave the DMP Detective Branch (DB) five days' remand in a Paltan police station case under the Prevention of Human Trafficking law; the article says his fourth remand day ended on Saturday and he was to be produced in court on Sunday.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report; DMP Additional Commissioner (DB) Md. Shafiqul Islam

facts.statement: DB Joint Commissioner Mohammad Nasirul Islam said a syndicate had formed in manpower export that deprived other validly licensed agencies and took extra money from workers going abroad; Masud Uddin Chowdhury's company was part of this syndicate and he is being questioned about it. The article does not name the company or the destination country.
facts.source_in_article: DB Joint Commissioner Mohammad Nasirul Islam

facts.statement: DMP Additional Commissioner (DB) Md. Shafiqul Islam said the DB is investigating the human trafficking case against Masud Uddin Chowdhury and that there are 10 more cases against him in Dhaka and Feni.
facts.source_in_article: DMP Additional Commissioner (DB) Md. Shafiqul Islam

facts.statement: Besides the trafficking case, Masud Uddin Chowdhury is being questioned about his role in the 11 January 2007 state of emergency and the arrest and torture of Tarique Rahman; sources say he has not admitted responsibility and blames DGFI officers. Former DGFI chief Lt Gen (retd) Sheikh Mamun Khaled was arrested by the DB on the following Wednesday and remanded five days in a Mirpur police station murder case.
facts.source_in_article: sources cited by Prothom Alo

headline_en: Government will help expatriates whose visas expire because of cancelled flights: expatriates' welfare minister
summary_en: Speaking in Sylhet on Saturday 7 March 2026, the expatriates' welfare minister said the ministry will help expatriates whose visas are expiring because flights were cancelled during the Middle East war, and that the ministry has opened a hotline. He said the ministry, the foreign ministry and civil aviation are working together, embassies are monitoring the situation, and deaths are being handled with the governments concerned. The rest covers law and order in Sylhet and a Holi event.

facts.statement: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said on 7 March 2026 that the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry will assist expatriates whose visas are expiring because their flights were cancelled (during the Middle East war); those who contact the ministry will be helped 'according to the government's capacity'. The article does not say what form the help takes.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, speaking to journalists in Sylhet

facts.statement: The Expatriates' Welfare Ministry has opened a hotline to help expatriates affected by the Middle East war situation, the minister said on 7 March 2026; the number is not printed in the article.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, speaking to journalists in Sylhet

facts.statement: The minister said the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry, the Foreign Ministry and Civil Aviation are working jointly on Bangladeshis in the Middle East; the ministry and embassies are regularly monitoring the countries where the war is ongoing; when news of a Bangladeshi killed in the war arrives, the government of the country concerned is informed at once and the regular procedure is followed.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, speaking to journalists in Sylhet

headline_en: Iranian attack now kills a Bangladeshi in Bahrain
summary_en: Abul Mohsin alias Tareq (52) of Sandwip, Chattogram, who worked at a company printed as 'RC Drydock' (আরসি ড্রাইডক) in Manama, Bahrain, was reported killed in an Iranian missile attack at about 3:30 am local time on Sunday 1 March 2026. He had gone to Bahrain in 2009. Earlier, a Bangladeshi named Saleh Ahmad died in an Iranian attack in Ajman, UAE on Saturday night.

facts.statement: Abul Mohsin alias Tareq (52), from Azimpur union, Sandwip, Chattogram, was reported killed in an Iranian missile attack in Bahrain at about 3:30 am local time on Sunday (1 March 2026); according to family citing relatives in Bahrain, he worked at a company named 'RC Drydock' (আরসি ড্রাইডক, as printed) in the capital Manama and the attack happened there at night.
facts.source_in_article: family members citing relatives in Bahrain; brother-in-law Riaz Uddin

facts.statement: Abul Mohsin went to Bahrain in 2009 and was the father of one daughter; his family learned of his death at about 6 am Bangladesh time on Monday 2 March 2026 and said efforts would be made to bring the body home. Sandwip police OC Abu Zayed Md. Nazmun Noor said police had learned of the death through various channels and were making enquiries.

headline_en: The risks created by the controversy over postal ballots
summary_en: An opinion column on expatriate postal voting after viral videos showed many postal ballots with Bahrain addresses being counted in one house, with similar videos from Saudi Arabia and Kuwait; the Election Commission is investigating. It explains how expatriate voting works (registration in the 'Postal Vote BD' app, ballot posted to the voter's foreign address and posted back), why shared addresses are common among migrant workers, the risk from third-party 'centres' filling in the app, and compares the Philippines, Mexico and Sri Lanka.

facts.statement: Bangladeshi expatriate voting is postal, not in-person voting at embassies: the voter registers/enrols in the Election Commission's official 'Postal Vote BD' app (which is for registration and ballot tracking), the ballot is posted to the voter's address abroad, and the voter marks it and posts it back to Bangladesh. The Commission's documents do not make the embassy a mandatory intermediary.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, North South University

facts.statement: The Election Commission warns that the address entered in the 'Postal Vote BD' app must be the address where the voter currently lives, with road, building and block/area written clearly and an accurate postal/ZIP code.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, North South University

facts.statement: Prothom Alo reported on 13 January 2026 that a video had spread showing many postal ballots bearing Bahrain addresses being counted in one house, with a request heard in the video not to spread it on Facebook; journalist Zulkarnain Saer then posted two more videos showing similar incidents in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, with migrant workers angry that some ballots were found with other people. Experts confirmed the videos were not fake or AI-made, and the Election Commission is investigating.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, North South University

facts.statement: The writer notes that in labour-receiving countries, especially in the Middle East, many workers share one house, flat or camp so one address serves many people; in Malaysia many Bangladeshi workers are irregular and lack a permanent address, valid tenancy agreement or regular postal access, so a colleague's or acquaintance's address is used as a 'common address'.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, North South University

facts.statement: Because many migrant workers have little education and struggle to write an address in English or understand postal codes, informal 'centres' or third parties in Bangladesh fill in online applications or the voting app for them; the writer warns this concentrates personal data, addresses and the whole voting process in a few hands. He does not report a proven fraud.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, North South University

facts.statement: The writer warns that suspicion of rigging in expatriate voting could break bonds among workers abroad and increase conflict, and that employing countries might reconsider taking workers from Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, North South University

facts.statement: Comparisons cited: the Philippines passed its overseas absentee voting law (Republic Act 9189) in 2003, amended by Republic Act 10590 in 2013, with voting generally through embassies/consulates and low turnout; Mexico's National Electoral Institute (INE) registers voters abroad and uses postal, remote and in some cases consular voting, where postal delivery and address problems limited participation; Sri Lanka has not yet decided on expatriate voting.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, North South University
